articles.title_zh: WARNS: China expert reveals what's at stake in America's reliance on China
articles.content_orig:
China has ‘wiretapped the Red Sea,’ ex-White House official warns as satellite images reveal new spy hub ahead of Xi visit.
Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a dangerous surveillance hub, a former Pentagon official warned Sunday, after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint just six miles from a key $66 million-a-year U.S. military base in Djibouti, Africa.
The report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) cited new facilities which it said would likely enable the Chinese military to monitor activities of other militaries operating nearby, although it also clarified it was not possible to determine whether China was actively intercepting communications.
The developments, one defense expert told Fox News Digital, could also inject fresh tension into U.S.-China relations in the run-up to Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House on Sept. 24. Beijing's intelligence-gathering capabilities are already under renewed scrutiny.
"What China is clearly doing is building eavesdropping capabilities. That seems to be their aim," said Morgan Murphy , former Trump White House official and press secretary for Mark Esper when he was secretary of defense during the first Trump administration.
CHINA-LINKED SPY SITE EXPANSION IN CUBA RAISES ALARMS NEAR KEY US MILITARY BASES
Morgan Murphy said it was significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from America's base in Djibouti. ( STR/AFP via Getty Images)
"Beijing has clearly wiretapped the Red Sea. When you build a 30-meter (100-foot-wide) satellite dish and cover it with a dome, so nobody can see where it's pointing, it's pretty clear you're up to no good," Murphy added while stating of the Washington-based think tank, that "the specificity here reflects the thorough research we expect out of CSIS."
The report pinpoints a large southeastern facility showing a control building, three 30-meter dipole antennas for high-frequency communications, two smaller antennas for very and "ultra-high frequencies," three mobile satellite dishes, four probable 5G towers and what CSIS said was a "radome" covering an unidentified asset.
CSIS also highlighted two new communications facilities that it says have emerged since 2024 that are likely to form part of a C4ISR command architecture, expanding China’s ability to intercept signals, track naval movements and communicate with Beijing while monitoring foreign militaries in the region.
The facilities would provide China with "a much more robust picture of the operating environment in the region," the report said.
CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES
CSIS said commercial satellite imagery revealed that China’s military had installed new antennas, satellite communications equipment and signals intelligence assets at its base in Djibouti — its only formally acknowledged overseas military installation. (Planet Labs / Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS))
"This isn’t a supply depot — it’s a 50-yard line seat over America’s power projection and the U.S. Navy," Murphy said before stating that the U.S. has "128 bases in more than 51 countries — China has just one."
"But look at the location — a few miles from Camp Lemonnier, overlooking the choke point that moves roughly a sixth of global sea trade. Great powers don’t plant listening posts next to rival fleets for 'logistics,'" he warned.
"Britain held Gibraltar to see who entered the Med while Japan’s island radios came before the runways. The Soviets’ overseas sites were never just about fuel and Beijing is running that playbook on the Red Sea," Murphy added.
Although China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jian said China is "unaware of the specific situation" and framed the country as a "builder of international peace," the new facilities provide Beijing with a picture of regional operations, according to Reuters.
CHINA IS BUILDING A MASSIVE SHIP THAT SHOULD SCARE AMERICANS ABOUT THE FUTURE
Beijing has transformed the Red Sea into a surveillance hub, former Pentagon officials warned after a new report revealed upgrades to China’s military footprint in Djibouti. ( DAPHNE BENOIT/AFP via Getty Images)
"The new report is helpful in framing the conversation, and it comes at an awkward time for China because Xi Jinping is visiting the White House on the 24th of this month," Murphy said.
"I'd bet a box of donuts this issue comes up. There is going to be public exposure of this, which Chinese leadership isn't used to. They aren't used to being asked tough questions by the press," he said.
President Donald Trump recently addressed Chinese intelligence efforts aboard Air Force One, acknowledging that China "spies on us" just as "we spy on them."
Trump's comments followed a report by The Wall Street Journal linking support from a Chinese entity to high-resolution satellite imagery used by Iran prior to a deadly missile attack on U.S. troops in Jordan.
"They basically do what we do," Trump noted, adding that "Xi has behaved reasonably well, and we behave reasonably well. ... You know what they say? That China spies on us. I say you're right, and we spy on them, too," he said, according to Reuters .
RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER
President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of a bilateral meeting at Gimhae Air Base on Oct. 30, 2025 in Busan, South Korea. Trump said he wants to keep the Strait of Hormuz open in the Middle East for countries, including China. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Murphy noted, "Nations spy on each other — allies and adversaries alike."
"It is a very old playbook, and listening posts all over the world are typical of great powers, but where the metal hits the floorboard is when you try to use that information," he said before adding that China may "keep tabs on us, but they cannot project power like the United States can."
The proximity of China's facility to U.S. operations is a core concern. Located less than six miles from Camp Lemonnier — the primary U.S. counterterrorism hub in Africa — and near French, Italian and Japanese installations, the site has a history of friction with U.S. forces.
"We are just right around the corner from China, and yet it's not a cooperative relationship," Murphy explained.
"Back in 2018, they lasered two of our C-130 pilots' eyes who suffered lasting damage from that incident. Beijing denied it, of course, but we know the truth."
WE SHOULD USE REAGAN AS A GUIDE IN HANDLING OUR MODERN ARMS RACE WITH CHINA
U.S. military aircraft as seen at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti. Camp Lemonnier is the only permanent United States military base in Africa. (Getty Images)
During the 2018 incident , the Pentagon had formally complained to China after military-grade lasers were pointed at American pilots attempting to land at Camp Lemonnier, causing minor injuries.
While Beijing dismissed the allegations as "groundless accusations," the confrontation underscored the potential for friction between military forces operating from nearby bases.
"China has one overseas base. The United States has more than 128 — by some counts, over 700 installations around the world," Murphy said.
"So it's significant that China has chosen to place its only overseas base six miles from ours in Djibouti. It is hugely strategically important, which is why, of course, we're there."
IS TRUMP CONSIDERING BOLD AFRICA PLAY TO PUSH BACK ON CHINA, RUSSIA AND ISLAMIC TERRORISTS?
The northwest facility at the Chinese base in Djibouti features a possible communications building and a "radome" with an unidentified asset, images show. (Planet Labs / Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS))
"It's our only base on the continent of Africa," he said, noting that it shares a "parking lot" with Japanese and Italian bases.

The U.S. and Iran are expected to have separate talks with mediators on Monday or Tuesday, an official with knowledge of the negotiations told the Reuters news agency.
With Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in the U.S., as well as Qatari mediators, the talks are set to focus on an updated version of the seven-day proposal Iran gave to U.S. counterparts last week during the United Nations General Assembly, the official told Reuters.
President Trump said Sunday that he expected talks with Iran to resume in the coming days , a day after he rejected a new proposal put forward by Tehran last week for a seven-day ceasefire and phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios . "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
Saudi Arabia has resumed exporting oil using its crucial East-West Crude Oil Pipeline after drone strikes earlier this month forced it shut, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter quoted by Bloomberg .
Saudi Arabia had been using the pipeline to transport oil from its eastern production hubs to its Red Sea ports for export — a vital alternative route as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has remained severely disrupted by the U.S.-Iran war.
The pipeline was shut down earlier this month after a series of drone attacks that Saudi authorities blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
The state-run energy giant Saudi Aramco, which operates the kingdom's oil infrastructure, tested the pipeline last week and has now resumed overseas shipments via the Red Sea route, a source familiar with the operation told Bloomberg.
Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have vowed to impose a blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports and against Saudi ships, and they have targeted several vessels in the region.
Iran has lodged a complaint with the United Nations over U.S. sanctions against its aviation sector, which have forced the cancellation of many flights across the region, state media reported Monday.
The U.S. imposed restrictions this month on the entire Iranian aviation industry and vowed to take a hard line against any companies or countries that continue to assist it.
As the sanctions took effect last Wednesday, some major airlines were forced to cancel international flights as several nations in the region implemented bans.
"To defend the legitimate rights of the aviation industry and counter illegal restrictions imposed by America, Iran has drafted and submitted a formal protest to the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO)," said civil aviation chief Abouzar Shiroudi, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has been quoted as predicting that U.S. military forces will soon be driven out of the Arabian Sea.
In a message to mark Iran's Sacred Defense Week, the ayatollah — who has not been seen or heard from directly since the war began — said U.S. forces were unable to advance beyond the Arabian Sea, which leads to the Strait of Hormuz, "because of the painful blows they have received."
He added that soon, U.S. troops would be driven from the Arabian Sea, too.
U.S. forces have operated across the region since the war began, including to escort commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in defiance of Iran's bid to control traffic through the vital waterway.
The wide-ranging message attributed by Iranian state media to Khamenei included praise for Iran's military forces, as well as for the former leader of the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon.
Khamenei was named Iran's new supreme leader soon after his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, was killed in the first round of U.S.-Israeli strikes, which sparked the war on Feb. 28.
The younger Khamenei has not been seen, even in video, since he was named the supreme leader, and senior U.S. officials have said he was likely seriously wounded in the same strike that killed his father.
The Iranian rial has fallen to a new historic low against the U.S. dollar, with the free-market selling rate surpassing 2.4 million rials per dollar on Monday.
Data from Pashizi, which tracks Iran's free-market exchange rates, put the dollar at around 2.4 million rials as Iran faces high inflation, sweeping sanctions and growing disruption to foreign trade.
Annual inflation has reached 61.4% in August, while food prices are reported to have risen 128% from a year earlier, according to data from Iran's Statistical Center.
Iranian state media said Monday that Iran's delegation at the U.N. General Assembly in New York had no plans to hold direct talks with the U.S., after President Trump said he expected more negotiations to take place this week.
"Iran's delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States," said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group.
Mr. Trump told Axios on Sunday he expected negotiations to continue this week, and added that the Iranian leaders were interested in reaching an agreement because they are "losing badly."
"Iran's views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the U.S. side ... via a Qatari mediator," IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday.
Since the outbreak of the war in February, negotiations between Tehran and Washington have occurred largely through mediators.
U.K. police said five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran were being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks.
RAF Fairford, a U.K. Royal Air Force base about 85 miles west of London in rural Gloucestershire, has been used by American bombers to conduct strikes against Iranian missile sites. The British government, under an agreement made under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, granted the U.S. permission to use Farford and other key U.K. bases provided it was only for strikes defined as defensive in nature.
Authorities are investigating a link between the arrests in Fairford and Iran as one possibility. Iranian authorities have declared all bases used to attack Iranian territory as legitimate targets.
President Trump praised those who were involved in making the arrests.
"It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. "We had them under view for a long time and we got them."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran was ready for either diplomacy or a return to fighting in the war sparked seven months ago by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. He said it is now up to President Trump to choose which direction to go.
"We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed, and I repeat, we stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Araghchi told NBC News' "Meet the Press."
"At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose," he said.
President Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to return to a ceasefire agreement that collapsed months ago as part of a seven-day plan that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.
Araghchi said Tehran would wait for an official response from mediators.
President Trump said Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, a day after he rejected a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."

A pair of giant pandas landed in Atlanta on Sunday morning as they begin their 10-year stay in the United States thanks to a partnership with China.
The pandas, named Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, took off from Chengdu in southwestern China on Sunday morning aboard a specially designated Boeing 777 cargo plane dubbed the "FedEx Panda Express."
Under a newly finalized arrangement between Zoo Atlanta and the China Wildlife Conservation Association, the Georgia facility becomes one of only three American zoological parks hosting giant pandas, joining California's San Diego Zoo and Washington, D.C.’s Smithsonian’s National Zoo.
"This is a thrilling day for Zoo Atlanta and a historic moment for the City of Atlanta, the state of Georgia, and beyond," Zoo Atlanta President and CEO Raymond B. King said in a statement. "We are elated to welcome Ping Ping and Fu Shuang and could not be more excited about sharing that joy with our Members, guests, city, and community in the coming weeks."
The public will need to wait before catching a glimpse of the pair, according to zoo representatives. Both animals are entering a month-long quarantine inside a biosecure zone located within the park’s freshly built giant panda facility. An official public debut date has yet to be finalized by park officials.
Chinese President Xi Jinping initially disclosed the delivery on Thursday amidst a three-day bilateral summit involving U.S. President Donald Trump . Sending the animals proved to be among the few tangible results resulting from the diplomatic visit, which featured mutual displays of cordiality without resolving any deep-seated disputes existing between both nations.
The arrival fills a vacancy created when Zoo Atlanta said goodbye to its previous resident pandas in 2024. Although the underlying bilateral agreement was made public in April, specific timeline details were previously omitted.
The 10-year loan contract guarantees Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will remain at Zoo Atlanta for a decade. Born in 2020, both animals previously resided at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding. The Xinhua News Agency noted that Ping Ping, a male, features distinct dark rings surrounding his eyes, whereas Fu Shuang, a female, possesses a slightly prominent forehead.
Beijing has long used pandas as diplomatic tools globally, utilizing loan arrangements as expressions of goodwill or allowing contracts to lapse when international tensions grow.
Xi previously described the loan program as demonstrating "friendship between the Chinese and Americans."

articles.title_orig: China, US agree to tariff cuts on $60 billion of goods including agriculture, household items
articles.title_zh: China, US agree to tariff cuts on $60 billion of goods including agriculture, household items
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — The U.S. and China are planning to reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each country, according to government announcements from both sides Monday.
The detailed lists includes mostly imports of toys, sports equipment and Christmas decorations by the U.S., while American agricultural products accounted for much of the far longer list of imports by China.
Washington has sought to reduce its record trade deficit with Beijing, as the Asian country exports far more to the U.S. than it imports. U.S. goods trade deficit with China was more than $202 billion last year.
"If we see the tariff cuts actually implemented before the holiday season, it could provide a welcome boost to U.S. consumption and to retailers," said Jacob Cooke, CEO at WPIC.
Cooke, whose company primarily helps U.S. brands sell in China, said that Beijing's import list includes fast-growing categories such as hair care and packaged pet food, where Chinese brands are highly competitive against U.S. offerings. "Every percentage point counts for price competitiveness and preserving margin."
However, it was not immediately clear when lower tariffs would take effect, and by how much the duties would go down. The U.S. and China last year slapped import tariffs effectively of over 40% and more than 30%, respectively, on each other.
The two countries limited further tariff increases after a one-year truce reached last fall. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said negotiators agreed to extend that truce to January.
Monday's announcement followed U.S. President Donald Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., last week. The two sides said the highly anticipated U.S.-China "Board of Trade" would consist of officials from both governments, and would meet at least once a quarter , with the top officials meeting "whenever necessary."
Lower tariffs could substantially boost trade, especially for highly competitive Chinese companies. Home goods seller Ryan Zhao, director of Jiangsu Green Willow Textile, expects sales in the second half of the year to grow by 30% from a year ago if tariff cuts are implemented.
Here's a select list of products set to benefit:
Plates, cups, bowls, serving dishes
Blankets (including electric ones) and rugs
Christmas-tree lamps and ornaments
Toys (including tricycles, but excluding items that connect to WiFi or Bluetooth)
Billiards balls, chalk and tables
Rackets for games, other than for "lawn-tennis or badminton"
Soccer balls, baseballs, softballs, lawn-tennis balls
Fish hooks and fishing line
Horses, donkeys, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, chickens for breeding
Frozen, fresh or chilled whole chickens or turkeys
Rabbit meat, excluding rabbit heads
Dried, smoked or salted beef
Live freshwater ornamental fish
Ice cream and other frozen products
—CNBC's Matthew Tan contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: Unprecedented test flight of SpaceX’s Starship lifts off and will aim for orbit
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Unprecedented test flight of SpaceX’s Starship lifts off and will aim for orbit
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX launched its massive Starship rocket early Monday, sending the spacecraft into orbit for the first time.
Starship reached orbit around 8:15 a.m. local time with SpaceX employees in attendance at the launch loudly cheering the milestone.
The Federal Aviation Administration told CNBC by email that it issued a "license authorization for the SpaceX Starship Super Heavy Flight 14 launch and reentry operations" on Sept. 26.
With the 14th test flight of Starship, Elon Musk's aerospace and defense company also planned to deploy 26 of its new Starlink V3 satellites. After the Starship reached orbit, SpaceX began to quickly release the satellites around 8:25 a.m. local time.
A livestream of the test flight on social network X, which is owned by SpaceX, showed the rocket taking off at 8:48 a.m. ET, or 7:48 a.m. local time, from the company town of Starbase, Texas.
The ship's booster made a "soft splashdown" off the coast of Starbase a few moments after launch, while the Starship spacecraft continued to climb with one of its vacuum engines going out in sub-orbital trajectory.
Starship is critical to SpaceX's expansion plans. The company is counting on the giant rocket to scale its Starlink , or Connectivity, business, which was its largest and only profitable segment as of the second quarter. SpaceX operates around 11,000 active satellites in orbit today, compared to roughly 650 for competitor Eutelsat OneWeb.
On SpaceX's earnings call in August, Musk said, "It's not out of the question that at some point, Starlink will deliver a majority of the world's internet, at least in countries where we're allowed to operate, which is the vast majority of countries."
One Starship rocket can carry 60 of SpaceX's new Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company said, representing about 20 times the capacity of a Falcon 9 launch.
SpaceX went public in June in the largest IPO on record and is now valued at about $2 trillion.
SpaceX has designed its Starship Super Heavy rocket and booster to be fully reusable, and to lift more cargo for less cost into orbit than any prior spacecraft. None of the 13 earlier test flights have been intended to make it into orbit, but with the 14th flight, SpaceX is hoping Starship will circle the planet.
The company is preparing Starship for a major NASA test flight next year, and intends to use the rocket to bring U.S. astronauts back to the moon's surface.
SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said during the All-In Summit earlier this month that the company also plans to use Starship to put "supercompute in space," launching "AI compute satellites" into orbit in 2027.
The company's new v3 satellites , which are produced at a SpaceX facility in Redmond, Washington, are equipped with solar arrays that generate twice as much power as prior generations. They are also larger, and designed to be more powerful, transmitting data more rapidly than earlier versions to Starlink subscribers.

articles.title_orig: Opinion | China is no longer just the world’s factory. It’s the HQ
articles.title_zh: Opinion | China is no longer just the world’s factory. It’s the HQ
articles.content_orig:
Manufacturing capacity is moving overseas but China, as a global hub for innovation and development, remains the ‘industrial brain’
The global electronics industry is entering a structural transition. For over two decades, China served as the dominant manufacturing centre, with an unmatched concentration of suppliers, skilled labour, infrastructure, logistics and engineering capabilities. That concentration is being diluted. But interpreting this as the decline of Chinese manufacturing would be a mistake.
According to the Boston Consulting Group (BCG), since 2017, the share of electronics manufacturers from China – Taiwan, Hong Kong and the mainland – with overseas production has risen to 56 per cent from 12 per cent. BCG based its analysis on 942 publicly traded companies with annual revenues above US$500 million, including 314 headquartered in China. This transformation is remarkable.

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

KYIV, Ukraine — Russia’s round-the-clock bombardment of targets in Ukraine killed at least seven people and wounded more than 50 others, officials said Monday.
Moscow’s forces pounded apartment buildings, offices, data centers and a building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine in downtown Kyiv.
The ceaseless Russian drone attacks on cities and towns aim to wear down Ukraine’s resistance and cripple the Ukrainian economy.
The attacks followed a week of diplomatic efforts at the United Nations to get traction for negotiations on ending Moscow’s invasion that began 4½ years ago.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov indicated Monday that the chances of making speedy headway on forging a peace settlement were bleak after recent Ukrainian attacks, including during recent parliamentary elections in Russia.
“Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months,” Peskov told reporters. “That is happening right now.”
Russian drone attacks on the Kyiv region killed four people and wounded eight, officials said.
A woman was killed in a Russian strike on Kyiv’s Shevchenkivskyi district on Monday afternoon, the Kyiv city military administration said. The strike hit the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, the latest cultural landmark in the capital to be damaged.
Russian forces also hit a pharmaceutical company and gas stations in Kyiv.
One drone struck an office center in central Dnipro during working hours Monday, killing three people and wounding at least 12, local authorities said.
A Russian strike on a nine-story apartment building in the northeastern city of Kharkiv wounded 43 people, including 11 children, Mayor Ihor Terekhov said.
Four people, including two teenage girls, were hurt when a Russian drone struck a residential area in northern Ukraine’s Chernihiv region on Sunday evening, said Viacheslav Chaus, head of the regional military administration.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces struck two data centers in Kyiv, as well as gas stations in the Ukrainian capital. A distribution hub belonging to the Nova Poshta postal service was struck in the southern city of Odesa, it said.
The Russian military also hit a cargo ship in the Black Sea and another one in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk, the ministry said. The strikes aim to curb Ukraine’s grain exports, though they may also create food shortages in countries that rely on Ukrainian imports.
The Russian aerial attacks regularly hit civilian areas. Moscow claims it targets only military-related sites.
Battlefield positions have changed little since last year, in part because swarms of drones severely restrict troop movements, but Kyiv’s forces launched a recent offensive, code-named Operation Vivaldi, on part of the 1,250-kilometer (800-mile) front line.
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps said Monday it had recaptured another 51 square kilometers (20 square miles) from the Russians, bringing the total to 176 square kilometers (68 square miles) since the offensive began several months ago.
The corps said that in order to break through Russian defenses, it converted Soviet-era BTR-60 armored personnel carriers into kamikaze vehicles that blew up the strongest Russian fortifications. The operation has also used ground robots to attack Russian positions.
The claimed breakthroughs came in the Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine, which the bigger Russian army has been trying in vain to conquer.
Russian officials made no immediate comment on the Ukrainian claim.
Russia’s Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said Russian troops captured the villages of Novovodiane in the Donetsk region and Ulanove in the northern Sumy region.
It was not possible to independently verify the claims.
Zelenskyy said long-range strikes on Russian soil hit two defense plants in the Tula and Voronezh regions and oil facilities in the Krasnodar region, all in southern and western Russia.
Ukraine’s long-range drones have repeatedly targeted Russian fuel depots and industrial plants that are a mainstay of Moscow’s economy and war effort.
Ukrainian drone attacks overnight started fires at three infrastructure facilities in Russia’s Krasnodar region, local emergency officials said Monday, without identifying the locations.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 254 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Pope Leo arrived in France on Friday, Sept. 25, starting a four-day tour across Paris, Lourdes, and Metz that includes speeches and a massive outdoor mass. (HOST BROADCASTER via Reuters.)
Pope Leo XIV began his visit to France on Friday for his fifth Apostolic Journey as Pontiff. The four-day trip marks the first formal papal visit to the country once called "the eldest daughter of the Church" since Pope Benedict XVI’s visit in September 2008.
French bishops announced the visit’s theme as "That the world may have life," and it comes as the officially secular nation is seeing an influx of new baptisms. So far this year, according to the Conference of Bishops of France, more than 21,000 adults have joined the Church, an increase driven by 18 to 25-year-olds.
"Pope Leo's visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave" of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters. "French Catholics are… saying ​loudly that they need the Church to find their way in these uncertain moments in world history."
POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL
The pope will visit Metz on Sept. 28, 2026 to conclude his four-day state and pastoral trip to France, which also includes stops in Paris and Lourdes. (Jean-Christophe Verhaegen / AFP via Getty Images)
The rise comes after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades, and said the Church had shown "deep, total and even cruel indifference" ​to victims. Stenger, who led the Diocese of Troyes from 1999 to 2020, told Reuters the scandals "have deeply wounded the Church and damaged its credibility."
In what is described as an unusual move, the Vatican press office announced Pope Leo will meet privately in Lourdes with seven of those victims as part of a message of healing and vulnerability.
SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS
The Vatican calls the trip, "a journey that unites faith and public engagement, memory and the future, with listening and bridge-building at its heart." After being greeted by French President Emmanuel Macron and a courtesy visit to Élysée Palace on Friday, Pope Leo is scheduled to make 15 speeches during his visit. He is expected to speak on several spiritual and societal themes, including the need to protect immigrants , the sick and unborn, and defend human dignity in the era of AI, and address themes of peace, culture, and unity.
President of France Emmanuel Macron and First Lady Brigitte Macron welcome Pope Leo XIV to Élysée Palace on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Tom Nicholson/Getty Images)
French bishops have expressed surprise at the level of interest in the visit. The Associated Press reports organizers for Pope Leo’s Saturday Mass at Paris’ Place de la Concorde, expecting up to 1 million people, have lengthened the security perimeter, extending the site beyond the 1.2-mile length of the Champs-Élysées, where Pope Leo will parade in the Popemobile.
Among his more noteworthy stops, Pope Leo will worship and speak on Sunday at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, one of Christianity’s most-visited pilgrimage destinations, especially popular with the sick. It is where an ailing Pope John Paul II , on his final foreign trip in 2004, delivered a forceful condemnation of abortion and euthanasia.
Pope Leo XIV attends the Welcome Ceremony at Paris Orly International Airport on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)
Pope Leo’s visit, however, comes after France’s recent national debate and subsequent passage of legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. That followed 2024 legislation enshrining abortion as a constitutional right .
POPE LEO PROMOTES ARCHBISHOP WHO BARRED PELOSI FROM COMMUNION TO ONE OF VATICAN'S HIGHEST COURTS
On Friday, Pope Leo will speak at the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, or UNESCO, headquarters in Paris. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni says Leo will likely reiterate his call for an AI slowdown and speak "with regard to the meaning of existence, to what makes human beings human and what does not."
The speech comes after the Pope’s May manifesto in which Leo warned of the dangers of AI and urged international regulation of the industry. His position again puts him at odds with President Trump, who has encouraged AI innovation so the U.S. can compete with and surpass China.
A crucifix stands in front of the Basilique Notre-Dame du Rosaire, its spire draped with a banner marking the upcoming visit of Pope Leo XIV, five days ahead of the pontiff's trip to the site as part of his apostolic journey to France, in Lourdes on Sept. 22, 2026.
Following his UNESCO visit, Pope Leo holds a prayer service at the newly-restored Cathedral of Notre-Dame, marking the first papal visit since a 2019 fire nearly destroyed one of France’s national landmarks.
He concludes his trip on Monday with a symbolic full-day visit to the border city of Metz, the birthplace of former French Prime Minister Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union. It is a backdrop the Vatican says the Pope will use to "champion friendship among European peoples."

Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Generations of artisans from Mumbai to Lucknow have shaped the world’s most coveted designs. Plus, the gen Z memes giving classic Bollywood a new life
T he zardozi embroidery on a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.
Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelier Chanakya International is at the forefront.
Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.
“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says, France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have in India today is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”
Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, or chaand jaal , reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.
In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing its partnership with Chanakya , in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.
These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. The Kalhath Institute , a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.
Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”
This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-based the Gem Palace , established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.
One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.
With increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collection attracted criticism after many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)
Then, Fendi came under fire when people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in a social media video showcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.
After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.
A recent Financial Times report noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.
Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, a controversy that showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.
Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection, Made in India , and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.
Might these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author of Inspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design , appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.
Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.
I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.
India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buy ajrakh and mashru silks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just a part of luxury, but a luxury itself.

U.S.-listed shares of global gold and silver miners dropped in premarket trading on the back of the retreat.

articles.content_orig:
Nvidia said Monday it has authorized an additional $150 billion to its share buyback program, taking its total to $235 billion, amid record spending on AI.
The chip giant said it marks the largest share repurchase authorization increase in history. It expects to complete the total remaining buyback program through the fiscal year 2028.
Nvidia produces the most advanced chips used for AI and has been a huge beneficiary of the boom in spending on the infrastructure needed to power the tech.
Nvidia's shares have climbed 24% over the past 12 months, lifting the company's market cap to $5.42 trillion. The stock was up 3.4% on Monday.
"NVIDIA's growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing," said CEO Jensen Huang in a statement.
"Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders," he added. "This authorization reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead."
Combined hyperscaler capital expenditure is projected to exceed $1.3 trillion by 2027, S&P Global Ratings said in August, as companies race to build AI infrastructure including data centers.
Huang earlier this month said Nvidia would double the number of chips it sells in 2027.
Alongside making the leading chips for AI — graphics processing units — including its Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems, the company makes a variety of additional semiconductors. That includes central processors, or CPUs, switch chips, chips for optical networking, chips for laptops, Jetson chips for robots and cars, and the chip inside Nintendo's Switch 2 gaming console.
"I think we're going through the largest infrastructure buildout in human history, and we have the benefit of being a very central part of that," Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday.
"We're going to generate a lot of cash in the coming years, and every single year, as we generate more cash, we'd like to be able to return it back to shareholders," he said.

U.K. police say they arrested multiple suspects for offenses under the "Explosives Act" near a U.S. airbase in southwest England on Sunday.

"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire Police said in a statement. "It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act."

"The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain. It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation," Trump said of the suspects. "They, they were looking to do big damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great."
A reporter then asked if the suspects were migrants, and Trump demurred.
"It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know that we worked with a lot of them. We had them under review for a long time and we got them," Trump said.

The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts," he added.

Minnesota officials have not publicly attributed the attacks. Several news outlets, citing U.S. officials and a leaked industry threat-sharing memo, reported that Iran was the likely culprit.

"Our condolences go out to Satterley's family, friends and fans," All Elite Wrestling wrote on social media.

articles.content_orig:
The 2026 MTV Video Music Awards wowed audiences on Sunday night as Madonna brought out high-energy dance numbers and Taylor Swift made history.
Here are the highlights from the 2026 VMAs.
Madonna took the VMAs stage at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles, her first time performing at the award show in over 20 years, announcing: "It's mother."
She opened the show with newly iconic imagery from her recent album, "Confessions II," including green lasers and hordes of cameras following her and Sabrina Carpenter around.
The two performed "Bring Your Love" together, which later won the Best Collaboration award, before Madonna transitioned into another dance-fueled club number, "Danceteria," with Charli XCX. The performance featured appearances from several stars who had cameos in "Confessions II — The Film," including Debi Mazar and Julia Garner.
Madonna later took home Artist of the Year.
Kacey Musgraves paid tribute to Dolly Parton on Sunday after the VMAs played a short video of the late country music superstar. Musgraves sang "I Will Always Love You," a song Parton released in 1974 that took on a second life when it was later recorded by the late Whitney Houston.
Parton, one of the most groundbreaking and successful musicians in the history of country music, died last month after a brief battle with cancer.
K-Pop star LISA performed her new single "SaWaDiKa" in the song's TV debut. Part of the performance included the singer riding in the front of Thailand's iconic tuk-tuk taxi.
Earlier in the night, she accepted the Best Pop award for "Dream feat. Kentaro Sakaguchi."
The surviving members of genre-defining grunge band Nirvana were given the Video Vanguard award, recognizing their contribution to the form.
The tribute included archival footage of late frontman Kurt Cobain discussing the process behind the making of several of the band's videos, including "Smells Like Teen Spirit," "Come As You Are" and "Heart-Shaped Box."
The VMAs also brought a milestone for Taylor Swift , who was given the VMAs' first-ever Artist Director Honor, which organizers said recognizes artists "whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling."
Swift thanked her fans and everyone she has ever collaborated with on her music videos. She then premiered the music vide o for her new single "Patient Zero," which stars Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell.
The new accolade, plus her other wins Sunday night, made Swift the show's most-awarded artist ever with 33 VMAs. She was previously tied with Beyoncé, who has 30 Moon Persons.
Swift also won Video of the Year and Best Direction, and was nominated in nine other categories. She paid tribute to "the ultimate showgirl" Dolly Parton in her acceptance speech for the final award of the evening.
"I think we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time," she said.
In addition to her opening performance, Madonna also collected a slew of Moon Persons on Sunday.
The Queen of Pop was nominated in 13 categories, the most of any artist, and went home with seven wins: Artist of the Year, Best Collaboration, Best Dance, Best Long Form Video, Best Album, Best Cinematography and Best Choreography.
She now has 27 VMAs across her career.
"It's been a while since I did one of these things," Madonna said when accepting her first award of the evening. "So, I've prepared nothing."
Later, when accepting the Artist of the Year award, she joked, "First of all, I would like to thank my fingers because I can always count on them."
Swift's three awards, including the Artist Director Honor, tied her with K-Pop stars BTS for second-most wins on the night.
Alex  Sundby contributed to this report.

British counterterrorism police are leading an investigation after five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses and preparing a terrorist act near an air base used by U.S. forces.
Police received a report at around 12:45 a.m. Sunday about three suspicious vehicles traveling toward RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England. Armed officers responded and arrested the men in nearby Whelford.
Fairford is used as a forward operating location for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command. The base has hosted U.S. B-52 and B-1 bombers during the Iran war , according to ABC News . American forces have used Fairford to carry out strikes against Iranian missile sites, the Associated Press reported.

In a press conference Sunday, Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said that about 85 households in the area were advised to evacuate early Sunday morning as a precaution.
"A 400m cordon has been put in place around the vehicles, while the Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit examine them,” Ocone said. A statement from police earlier Sunday said that they believe the situation is “contained.”
Aerial footage from Sky News shows a bomb disposal robot moving between three white vans at the site, with the rear doors of two vehicles open.
Ocone added that the men remain in custody and will be questioned by police.
The base is home to both the 501st Combat Support Wing Headquarters and the 420th Air Base Squadron, and serves as the “preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe,” according to the U.S. Air Force.
TIME has reached out to the U.S. Air Force for comment on the incident.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who assumed the post in July, called the incident “deeply concerning” on X .
“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” he wrote. “The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.” When asked by reporters about the arrests, U.S. President Donald Trump called them “fantastic.” “They were looking to do big damage to our fort,” Trump said of the suspects, “and working with the British worked out great.”
Trump also said the suspects had been under surveillance before their arrests. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he said.
British police have not confirmed that RAF Fairford was the intended target of the suspected attacks. The Associated Press reported that investigators were considering a possible connection to Iran, but no such link has been confirmed.

In late summer, when almond husks split open, workers at Creekside Farming in Madera gear up machinery to shake the trees. Tractors zoom around, fallen nuts are collected, and trucks cart off the bins of almonds.
The whole process relies on diesel fuel, which has grown extremely expensive in recent months, said farm owner Jay Mahil, whose family has been growing wine grapes, citrus and other crops in the Central Valley for four generations.
The national average price of diesel hit a new record high of $5.85 per gallon Friday, while California’s average climbed to about $7.71, according to the AAA motor club.
The oil product undergirds much of the global economy, and California, a major player, is no exception to the pain caused by ongoing supply chain disruptions stemming from the U.S.  war with Iran.
The higher fuel costs are squeezing businesses across various industries in California, which has massive trucking and agricultural sectors that rely heavily on diesel to power equipment.
Mahil said his fuel costs are up 40% from this time last year.
“These higher costs come at the worst time for us, “ Mahil said. “These are highly inundated time frames.”
Mahil keeps a close eye on prices. When there’s an occasional slump or dip in the oil market, he orders several truckloads of fuel. But other businesses usually have the same idea, and the fuel depots often run out those days.
“We are running a little leaner right now, with less oil in the tanks,” Mahil said.
California diesel prices set a  record earlier on in the war, at around $7.75 per gallon in April.
Greg Dubuque, general manager for a trucking fleet based out of Montebello, noted that the cost to fill his trucks in California has gone from around $1,200 in April to $1,800.
“It’s a dramatic impact, especially for us smaller companies,” he said.
Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, said more than two-thirds of cargo moving in and out of the port is carried by trucks. And of the some 1,200 trucking companies that do business at the port, more than 50% are small to medium-sized companies that are seriously struggling with prices, Seroka said.
“It’s difficult for companies to absorb such an energy shock as we’ve seen over the past six months,” Seroka said.
The turmoil in the Persian Gulf region is forcing cargo away from the Suez Canal and onto a longer route around the southern tip of Africa, creating longer transit times that burn more fuel and drive costs up further, Seroka said.
Increased diesel prices are  pushing up the cost to transport food. Frozen and refrigerated goods, such as fresh produce, are most sensitive to price increases because diesel is typically used to power both cold storage and transportation.
Nick Vyas, a supply chain expert and professor at USC Marshall School of Business, said that while companies try to absorb some of the cost increase, grocery prices are starting to tick up in stores.
Though grocery costs may decrease slightly once fuel costs stabilize, they are unlikely to return to  prewar baselines as retailers adjust to higher prices, Vyas noted, pointing to sustained increases in food costs post-pandemic.
With American refiners funneling the fuel oil into international markets, the domestic supply has dwindled, driving up prices. Diesel prices jumped 7 cents overnight, 24 cents in the past week, 48 cents in the past month and $2.14 compared with this time last year, according to AAA.
Kandace Redd, a AAA spokesperson, said the organization’s past research shows that consumers are most likely to drive less, combine errands and reduce shopping or dining out to cope with record pump prices.
Diesel prices in California are typically above the national average as the state faces cost pressures from higher taxes and environmental standards, Vyas said. Because around 40% of goods imported in the U.S. pass through the San Pedro and Long Beach ports, California’s energy costs also expose the rest of the nation’s supply chain to these increases.
Larger companies are better poised to absorb some of the shock of increased prices through higher profit margins and the ability to buy in bulk, Vyas said. Mom-and-pop businesses, such as small trucking fleets or family farms, are hit harder.
“When you’re a large national truckload carrier, the J.B. Hunts and the Swifts and the Werners of the world, they do a lot of hedging on fuel,” meaning they establish advance agreements to purchase fuel at a fixed cost, Dubuque said.
His smaller fleet of 40 trucks, on the other hand, is generally stuck paying the price at the pump.
Dubuque is taking several steps to try and mitigate the impact. This includes explaining the rising cost of doing business to his customers, avoiding refueling in California where possible and using alternative fuels to power air conditioning in trucks overnight.
But as the manager of a smaller company, he is nervous about how long these strategies will work if diesel prices don’t start dipping.
A similar disparity is seen when it comes to the impact of rising diesel prices on consumers, Vyas noted. For low-income households, any uptick in grocery prices will stretch already strained budgets, while wealthier consumers may not notice the change.
Economist Christopher Thornberg has a more optimistic outlook on the impact of rising fuel prices on the average consumer. He pointed out that fuel prices have been notably low in recent years. He said the current diesel spike is not exceptionally high when put in the context of inflation-adjusted averages over the last two decades.
“Sure, it’s a shock from where it was six months ago, but from a long-run perspective, once you control for price growth, it’s not a big deal,”  said Thornberg, founding partner of Beacon Economics.
Inflation-adjusted diesel prices have reached higher than the current $5.85 national average per gallon. The 2008 peak of $4.74 a gallon is equivalent to $7.20 in today’s dollars, while the more recent 2022 peak of almost $5.82 would be about $6.56 today.
And while certain industries  such as trucking remain reliant on diesel fuel, alternative energy sources and increased domestic oil production have made the American economy as a whole less sensitive to fluctuations in global fuel prices compared  with past energy crises, he noted.
Nonetheless, news of a  record high in national diesel prices is likely to disturb consumers and carry political ramifications for the  Trump administration, Thornberg said.
AP-NORC polling shows that around two-thirds of Americans disapprove of  the president’s handling of the economy. The continued surge in diesel and oil prices is unwelcome news for the Republican Party heading into November’s midterm elections.

The high-altitude reconnaissance platform took part in exercises around the disputed South China Sea flashpoint
Beijing deployed its advanced WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drone in the South China Sea for the first time during drills near the disputed Scarborough Shoal on Sunday.
The People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theatre Command announced on Sunday that it had conducted joint air and naval exercises in the waters and airspace around the shoal earlier in the day.
In recent years, Scarborough Shoal – known as Huangyan Island in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines – has been a major flashpoint between the two countries, which both claim ownership of the coral atoll.

Ted Kaczynski was 16 when he entered Harvard University as a mathematics prodigy. Years later, he would become known as the Unabomber, after carrying out a bombing campaign that killed three people and injured 23 others between 1978 and 1995.
Netflix’s Unabomber directed by Janus Metz, explores Kaczynski’s life before and during the events that led to his capture. Jacob Tremblay plays the younger Kaczynski, while Russell Crowe portrays Harvard professor Henry Murray, Shailene Woodley plays FBI agent Joanne Miller and Annabelle Wallis portrays Christiana Morgan, Murray’s academic collaborator.
“We decided to explore Ted Kaczynski's time at Harvard, as it stood out as a formative and fragile period in his life,” Metz tells TIME. “We wanted to understand who this young man was up until he began his descent into a darker and deadlier path.”
Born in Chicago in 1942, Kaczynski demonstrated exceptional mathematical ability from an early age. He entered Harvard at 16 before continuing his studies at the University of Michigan, where he earned a master’s degree and a doctorate in mathematics.
At 25, he became a professor at the University of California, Berkeley. But he left the university in 1969 and eventually moved to a remote cabin near Lincoln, Mont., where he lived without electricity or running water.
Kaczynski became increasingly isolated from society. He spent much of his time reading, hunting and growing plants, while developing increasingly strong opposition to modern technology and industrial society.
In 1978, Kaczynski began the bombing campaign that would eventually span nearly two decades. His first known attack involved a homemade device mailed to a professor at Northwestern University. It exploded when opened by a campus security officer, causing minor injuries. In November 1979, Kaczynski placed a device aboard an American Airlines flight, causing smoke inhalation injuries and forcing the plane to make an emergency landing.
Over the years, his targets included universities, airlines and people he associated with technology and the modern industrial system.
The FBI used the case identifier UNABOM, short for “University and Airline Bombing,” before Kaczynski’s identity was known. The media later used it to name him the “Unabomber.” Between 1978 and 1995, 16 attacks were linked to the case, killing Hugh Scrutton, Thomas Mosser and Gilbert Murray and injuring 23 people.
Kaczynski’s identity remained a mystery for years. That changed in 1995, when he sent a lengthy manifesto titled “Industrial Society and Its Future”  to The Washington Post and The New York Times and demanded that it be published. The approximately 35,000-word text laid out his opposition to modern technological society and explored ideas about human freedom, autonomy, and the effects of industrialization.
The FBI supported the decision to publish the manifesto in the hope that someone familiar with Kaczynski’s writing would recognize it. That person turned out to be his brother David’s wife, Linda Patrik.
After reading the manifesto, Patrik noticed similarities between its ideas and the writing she had previously seen from Kaczynski. She brought her concerns to David, who initially struggled to believe that his brother could be responsible for the attacks.
David eventually examined the manifesto alongside an essay Kaczynski had written years earlier. The similarities in their language and ideas were striking enough for him to contact the FBI.
The material gave investigators a crucial lead. After years of attacks and an extensive investigation, Kaczynski was now directly connected to the manifesto and the writings that could help identify him as the person behind the Unabomber case.
Shailene Woodley in Unabomber Courtesy of Netflix
On April 3, 1996, nearly two decades after the first attack, federal agents surrounded Kaczynski’s remote cabin near Lincoln, Mont., and arrested him.
The search of the property gave investigators a trove of evidence. Inside, they found bomb-making materials, a typewriter, coded diary entries and approximately 40,000 pages of handwritten notes, along with a completed bomb.
Kaczynski later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life in prison without parole. He remained incarcerated until his death in 2023 at age 81.
While in prison, Kaczynski was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia by a psychiatrist who interviewed him. He rejected the idea that he was mentally incapable of understanding his actions. In a 1999 interview with TIME , he said he was certain he was sane.
While at Harvard, Kaczynski took part in psychological experiments overseen by professor Henry Murray. Murray worked with Christiana Morgan at the Harvard Psychological Clinic, where they developed the Thematic Apperception Test, or TAT.
“Christiana was the co-creator of the Harvard school of psychology where the tests on Ted Kaczynski took place,” says Wallis, who plays Morgan in the movie. “Murray and Morgan were collaborators at the time and together devised the highly controversial stress tests used on Harvard students. I was fascinated to learn about the extent of her involvement.”
The experiments involved students writing about their beliefs before undergoing intense psychological sessions. They later became an important part of discussions about Kaczynski’s life, although their precise impact on him remains uncertain.
The full Harvard file on Kaczynski remains classified, making it impossible to know exactly what Murray concluded from the experiments.
“I don't think the Murray experiments in themselves turned Ted Kaczynski into the Unabomber,” says Metz. “There are many factors in Ted Kaczynski's life that contributed to his evolution.”
However, Metz says the experiments were designed to break down participants who knew very little about what they were being subjected to, and that the filmmakers wanted to show them as “likely a piece of the puzzle.”
Metz also points to Kaczynski’s own writings as another part of the story.
“We also know from Ted Kaczynski's own journals that he wanted revenge from feeling disrespected and rejected, which these experiments could have contributed to,” he says.
According to Metz, Kaczynski himself later claimed that the experiments had not had a significant effect on him.
Russell Crowe and Jacob Tremblay in Unabomber Courtesy of Netflix
For Tremblay, one of the challenges of playing Kaczynski was the lack of detailed information about his early life.
“While there is plenty of information to go off of from Ted's adult life, it was challenging to find material regarding his early life when I played him,” Tremblay says. “I was left with a rather blank canvas in terms of how much freedom I would have with the character.”
Tremblay listened to recordings of Kaczynski’s interrogation after his arrest to study his speech patterns and watched footage of him as an adult, noting his stiff posture. I then put my own youthful, nervous and softer spin on that,” Tremblay says.
The psychological experiment scenes presented a different challenge. Tremblay was strapped to a chair, limiting his movement and expressions. “I learned to utilize that unfamiliar and uncomfortable environment to my advantage,” Tremblay says. “Because Ted himself in that moment is also experiencing that discomfort and unfamiliarity at the same time.”
Unabomber is grounded in documented events from Kaczynski’s life, but the film also takes creative liberties with gaps in the historical record.

articles.title_zh: Nvidia launches AI safety platform after Jensen Huang calls Anthropic, OpenAI warnings 'odd'
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia has unveiled a new security platform designed to prevent AI agents from going rogue
Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue .
The company said that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open source software that “sets boundaries for agents,” and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations.
The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control.
Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face .
“From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," said the company’s vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI.
The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed the safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI's models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own.
Nvidia's software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said.
Because it's open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel.
The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can "intervene instantly" if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said.
“It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said.
“OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” Boitano said.
Nvidia said more than 100 organizations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture, and JPMorgan Chase.
The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. But others including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release.
Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address.
Also Monday, Nvidia said its board approved expanding its share repurchase program by $150 billion, raising the total amount to $235 billion.

Ukraine’s Third Army Corps has regained 51 square kilometers and five settlements during the third phase of Operation Vivaldi, bringing the total territory retaken in the offensive to 176 square kilometers.
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps liberated the settlements of Nove, Ridkodub, and Katerynivka and restored control over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka during the third phase of Operation Vivaldi.
According to the corps on September 28, Ukrainian forces regained another 51 square kilometers of territory during the latest phase, bringing the total area retaken since the start of its offensive operations to 176 square kilometers.

The Third Army Corps said Russian forces lost around 2,000 personnel during the operation, while more than 250 Russian troops were taken prisoner. The corps described the third phase, or “season,” of Vivaldi as a turning point in the broader operation.
The main objective of the third phase was Nove, which the corps described as a key Russian hub on the bridgehead. Third Army Corps Commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi said control of the surrounding high ground was crucial to maintaining the initiative in the area.
“The enemy was convinced that the main direction of the attack was Shandryholove–Zelena Dolyna. This forced them to senselessly burn through their reserves in counterattacks precisely in this direction. The Russians missed the real strike, which was focused on taking Nove,” Biletskyi said.
According to the corps, Ukrainian forces used modified Soviet-era BTR-60 armored personnel carriers to break through Russian defenses. The vehicles had been converted into remotely operated strike ground systems and were used to destroy heavily fortified Russian positions.
The Third Army Corps also said Russian troops surrendered in groups during the operation, including officers, drone pilots, and artillery personnel.
Operation Vivaldi was announced by Biletskyi on September 15 as a Ukrainian counteroffensive in northern Donetsk region. During its first phase, Ukrainian forces cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltration positions, regained control of several settlements, and reportedly inflicted substantial losses on Russian forces.
The operation has also involved new approaches to the use of unmanned systems. On September 24, the Third Army Corps said it carried out what it described as the first attack of its kind involving unmanned ground vehicles deployed by heavy bomber drones.
According to the corps, heavy bomber drones operated by the Third Assault Brigade carried NC13 strike UGVs, known as “Gryphons,” and deployed them more than 10 kilometers behind Russian lines.

articles.title_orig: Bangkok’s flood disaster – in pictures | Thailand
articles.title_zh: Bangkok’s flood disaster – in pictures | Thailand
articles.content_orig:
Capital city submerged in waist-high flood water, while elsewhere Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii’s Big Island
Bangkok was declared a disaster zone by its city officials towards the end of last week, after streets in Thailand’s capital city were submerged in up to waist-high flood water. The flooding stemmed from an active cell of low pressure across central Thailand that brought continuous heavy rainfall and thunderstorms to Bangkok and surrounding regions.
The heavy rain began early on Thursday when the weak area of low pressure travelled north-westwards up the gulf of Thailand before then sitting over central Thailand by Friday morning. For most of the following two days this low pressure remained roughly in situ, which allowed unrelenting downpours over Bangkok and nearby areas. One weather station near Prachin Buri, just north-east of the capital, recorded 213.5mm within a 24-hour period between Friday and Saturday evening local time – for comparison, London receives an average 585mm a year ). Fortunately, the centre of the low-pressure cell shifted north-westwards on Sunday and brought an end to the torrential rainfall.
Out in the central Pacific, meanwhile, citizens of Hawaii’s Big Island were threatened by Hurricane Nolo over the weekend. The system initially approached the archipelago early last week, bringing heavy rainfall from around Tuesday evening. By the early hours of Saturday Nolo was a category 2 hurricane, with sustained windspeeds of 85-90knots (98-104mph), situated at its closest to the archipelago at approximately 145 miles (233km) south of the Big Island. Strong winds were not the only threat to the Big Island, as the vast quantity of rainfall raised concerns over flooding and mudslides. Since the impacts of Nolo started late on Tuesday 22 September, weather stations in the north-east of the island have received over 530mm of rainfall. Fortunately, Nolo has propagated westwards away from Hawaii where it is forecast to peak in its intensity on Monday 28 September, with current predictions of achieving category 4 status.

Meanwhile, farther east in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is now forecast to make landfall with the Baja California peninsula late in the day on Monday 28 September. The once category 5 hurricane will downgrade to category 2 by landfall with sustained winds of 96-110mph. A hurricane warning has been issued in coastal regions due to the risk of a storm surge where winds are onshore. Polo will also bring intense downpours while traversing the peninsula with 100-200mm expected, potentially reaching up to 250mm locally. The bulk of this rain falling within a 12-hour period and bringing the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. The storm will continue to weaken while propagating north-eastwards across the Sonora region in Mexico.
